name: Ch’ēn T’ao
bio: Ch’ēn T’ao is dated by Giles to the 9th and 10th centuries AD. His poem here is an oath of soldiers on the frontier.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poems.title: An Oath
poems.author: Ch’ēn T’ao
poems.text:
They swore the Huns should perish: they would die if needs they must
And now five thousand, sable-clad, have bit the Tartar dust.
Along the river-bank their bones lie scattered where they may,
But still their forms in dreams arise to fair ones far away.

poems.title: Turkestan
poems.author: Ch’ēn T’ao
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)
poems.text:
Thinking only of their vow that they would crush the Tartars —
On the desert, clad in sable and silk, five thousand of them fell. . . .
But arisen from their crumbling bones on the banks of the river at the border,
Dreams of them enter, like men alive, into rooms where their loves lie sleeping.
